title: What HVAC Systems Qualify for a Tax Credit?
h1: What HVAC Systems Qualify for a Tax Credit?
description: The federal HVAC tax credit for heat pumps, AC and furnaces ended after 2025. See what qualified, who can still claim it and other ways to lower costs.
quick_answer: The federal Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit covered qualifying heat pumps, central air conditioners, gas furnaces and some related upgrades, but under current law it doesn't apply to equipment placed in service after December 31, 2025. Systems installed in 2025 may still be claimed on that year's return. Utility and state rebate programs may still help.
body:
Tax rules for home energy upgrades changed recently, so a lot of what you'll read online is out of date. Here's a plain summary of what the federal credit covered, where things stand now, and what still makes sense when you're choosing a new system. We aren't tax advisors, so confirm your situation with a tax professional before you count on any credit.

What did the federal HVAC tax credit cover?

The Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit, often called the 25C credit, applied to upgrades on your existing main home. For heating and cooling, it covered equipment that met high efficiency tiers set by the Consortium for Energy Efficiency, including:

  • Air source heat pumps, including many ductless mini splits
  • Central air conditioners
  • Natural gas, propane or oil furnaces
  • Heat pump water heaters
  • Some related upgrades, such as electrical panel work needed to support qualifying equipment and home energy audits

Geothermal heat pumps fell under a separate credit, the Residential Clean Energy Credit.

Is the HVAC tax credit still available?

Under the federal law passed in 2025, the Energy Efficient Home Improvement Credit doesn't apply to property placed in service after December 31, 2025. The geothermal credit also ended for expenditures made after that date. So for a system installed in 2026, there's generally no federal tax credit to claim.

Tax law can change again, and how the rules apply depends on your situation. A tax professional can tell you what applies to you.

What if your system was installed in 2025?

If qualifying equipment was installed and placed in service in 2025, you may be able to claim the credit on your 2025 return. If you already filed and missed it, ask a tax preparer whether amending makes sense. You'll typically need:

  1. Your invoice showing the equipment and install date
  2. The model numbers of the indoor and outdoor equipment
  3. The manufacturer's certification that the equipment qualified

Contact the company that did your install if you need copies of the paperwork.

Are there other incentives for new HVAC equipment?

Federal credits aren't the only option. Depending on the time and program, homeowners in San Diego and Orange County may find:

  • Rebates from your electric or gas utility for high-efficiency equipment
  • California programs that encourage switching from gas heating to heat pumps
  • Manufacturer promotions on certain equipment
  • Local offers from contractors

These programs open, change and run out of funding, so check what's current before you buy. You can see our current offers on the specials page.

Is an efficient system still worth it without a credit?

Often, yes. A tax credit was a one-time benefit. Lower monthly bills and better comfort last for the life of the system. When comparing equipment, look at:

  • SEER2 for cooling efficiency
  • HSPF2 for heat pump heating efficiency
  • AFUE for gas furnace efficiency
  • Two-stage or variable-speed operation, which improves comfort and humidity control

In mild coastal areas where the AC runs less, the most expensive high-efficiency system may not pay off as quickly as it would in a hot inland valley. A good estimate weighs your actual use, not just the efficiency rating.

Which features matter most in our climate?

San Diego and Orange County cover a wide range of conditions. Coastal homes see mild summers, damp mornings and cool winter nights, while inland valleys get hot afternoons for months. That affects which upgrades give you the most for your money:

  • Inland homes with heavy AC use tend to benefit most from higher SEER2 ratings and variable-speed equipment.
  • Coastal homes often care more about humidity control and quiet operation than top-tier cooling efficiency.
  • Homes switching from a gas furnace to a heat pump should check whether the electrical panel can handle the new load.
  • Attic duct systems are worth inspecting in every case, since duct leaks waste energy no matter how efficient the equipment is.

How do you choose the right system?

Start with a proper sizing calculation for your home, then compare equipment options at a few efficiency levels. Ask about ductwork condition, since leaky attic ducts can waste much of what an efficient system saves. Our HVAC installation team can walk you through options with a free estimate.
faqs: Can I still get a federal tax credit for a heat pump installed in 2026?
Under current federal law, the home improvement credit doesn't apply to heat pumps placed in service after December 31, 2025. Check with a tax professional in case the rules change.
Was the tax credit a rebate?
No. A tax credit reduced the federal income tax you owed when you filed. A rebate is money paid back to you, usually by a utility, the state or a manufacturer, and works differently.
Did every new AC qualify for the credit?
No. Only equipment that met specific high efficiency tiers qualified. Standard efficiency systems did not. The manufacturer's certification shows whether a model met the requirements.
Are there still rebates for heat pumps in California?
State and utility programs have offered heat pump incentives, but funding and rules change often. Check current programs before you buy, and ask your installer what's available at the time.
